# Digest R0 — Provan, *1 and 2 Kings* (NIBC): Front matter + Introduction

**Source:** Iain W. Provan, *1 and 2 Kings*, NIBC (Hendrickson/Paternoster 1995; Baker ebook 2012)  
**Slice:** `.cache/provan-kings-reingest-2026-07-18/slices/R0_front_intro_221-528.txt`  
**Raw line range:** 221–528  
**Coverage note:** Foreword (Hubbard & Johnston), Preface (Provan), Abbreviations (skipped — reference list only), full Introduction (narrative / historiographical / didactic; composition; typology; themes of promise). Slice file lines 1–308 map to this raw range (slice L1 ≈ raw L221). Loci below use **section markers** plus **slice lines** (and raw = 220 + slice line where useful).

### C-R0-01
**Claim:** Series editors Hubbard and Johnston position NIBC as “believing criticism”: probing, reflective interpretation married to loyal biblical devotion and warm Christian affection—not precritical paraphrase, anticritical defense, or criticism that brackets the meaning the text conveys.
**Quote:** "we have sought to align this series with what has been labeled believing criticism. This approach marries probing, reflective interpretation of the text to loyal biblical devotion and warm Christian affection."
**Locus:** Foreword; slice L17–19 (raw ~237–239)
**Targets:** [[provan-1-2-kings-nibc]], [[iain-provan]]

### C-R0-02
**Claim:** For the editors, NIBC contributors combine modern critical methodologies with commitment to the Bible’s full authority for Christians, aiming to illumine minds and deepen faith for academy and church.
**Quote:** "The authors in this series combine a firm commitment to modern scholarship with a similar commitment to the Bible’s full authority for Christians."
**Locus:** Foreword; slice L21
**Targets:** [[provan-1-2-kings-nibc]]

### C-R0-03
**Claim:** Provan wrote the commentary largely during sabbatical leave from the University of Edinburgh in summer 1993; he thanks Graeme Auld as a stimulating dialogue partner on Kings and notes reading Auld’s advance copy of *Kings Without Privilege* (T. & T. Clark, 1994).
**Quote:** "This commentary, for example, was largely written during a period of sabbatical leave from the University of Edinburgh in the summer of 1993"
**Locus:** Preface; slice L51
**Targets:** [[iain-provan]], [[provan-1-2-kings-nibc]], [[1-2-kings]]

### C-R0-04
**Claim:** Provan’s citation policy in the commentary’s additional notes is deliberately selective: only certain very recent books/articles on important interpretive points not already taken into account by previous Kings commentators; general indebtedness to prior scholarship is acknowledged in the preface without full bibliography of everyone.
**Quote:** "My general policy has been to cite in the additional notes to each section of the commentary only certain very recent books and articles that touch upon what I consider important points of interpretation and that have not been taken into account by previous commentators on Kings."
**Locus:** Preface; slice L55
**Targets:** [[provan-1-2-kings-nibc]], [[iain-provan]]

### C-R0-05
**Claim:** Provan treats 1 and 2 Kings as one book (“the book” of Kings), not two isolated books; the commentary will consistently refer to it as singular.
**Quote:** "First and Second Kings represent two parts of what must clearly be thought of as one book. Kings will consequently be referred to throughout this commentary as “the book” rather than “the books” of Kings."
**Locus:** Introduction opening; slice L231
**Targets:** [[1-2-kings]], [[provan-1-2-kings-nibc]], [[iain-provan]]

### C-R0-06
**Claim:** For Provan, Kings is not a self-contained entity: it presupposes Samuel (LXX title “1–4 Reigns” for Samuel-Kings), Joshua and Judges (Jewish “Former Prophets” for Joshua–Kings), and the Pentateuch (particularly Deuteronomy), and invites reflection in light of prophetic and other OT writings.
**Quote:** "it constantly presupposes knowledge of the story of Israel thus far, whether in Samuel (its close connection to which is well captured in the LXX title “1–4 Reigns” for Samuel-Kings); in Joshua and judges (cf. the traditional Jewish designation “The Former Prophets” for Joshua-Kings); or in the Pentateuch (particularly Deuteronomy)."
**Locus:** Introduction opening; slice L231
**Targets:** [[1-2-kings]], [[iain-provan]]

### C-R0-07
**Claim:** Provan asserts that a truly Christian reading of Kings requires reflection on its meaning in the total canonical context of the Christian Bible—“The Book is the environment in which the individual book must be read.”
**Quote:** "Indeed, a truly Christian reading will involve reflection upon the meaning of Kings in the total canonical context of the Christian Bible. The Book is the environment in which the individual book must be read."
**Locus:** Introduction opening; slice L231
**Targets:** [[1-2-kings]], [[iain-provan]], [[provan-1-2-kings-nibc]]

### C-R0-08
**Claim:** Provan’s threefold characterization of Kings: (1) narrative literature; (2) literature with historiographical intent (story about the past); (3) didactic literature teaching about God and the ways of God. The Introduction structures around these three.
**Quote:** "The book of Kings tells us a story; it is narrative literature. It is a story that is certainly about the past (whatever else it may also be about); it is literature with historiographical intent. It is, finally, didactic literature—it seeks to teach its readers a number of things about God and the ways of God."
**Locus:** Introduction; slice L233
**Targets:** [[1-2-kings]], [[iain-provan]], [[provan-1-2-kings-nibc]]

### C-R0-09
**Claim:** As narrative, Kings presents main characters (the LORD, Israelite kings and prophets, significant foreigners) though prominence is not always given to main characters; plot concerns Israel’s attempt (or failure) under monarchy to live as people of God in the land and how God deals with them.
**Quote:** "The plot is concerned with the attempt that Israel makes (or more often, does not make) under its monarchy to live as the people of God in the promised land and with how God deals with the Israelites in their success and failure."
**Locus:** Intro “The Book of Kings as Narrative Literature”; slice L237
**Targets:** [[1-2-kings]], [[kingship-in-israel]], [[iain-provan]]

### C-R0-10
**Claim:** Provan frames the narrative arc from David (1 Kgs 1:1) to Zedekiah (2 Kgs 25:7), with an epilogue for Jehoiachin (25:27–30), ordered by each reign’s place in the book’s framework of regnal formulae.
**Quote:** "It is a plot worked out gradually, as king succeeds king, from David (1 Kgs. 1:1) to Zedekiah (2 Kgs. 25:7), with an epilog reserved for Jehoiachin (25:27–30)"
**Locus:** Intro Narrative; slice L237
**Targets:** [[1-2-kings]], [[david]], [[kingship-in-israel]], [[iain-provan]]

### C-R0-11
**Claim:** Provan describes characteristic regnal formulae (accession timing relative to another king, length of reign, capital, death/burial, successor, source notice, religious-policy evaluation; for Judean kings also mother’s name and age at accession) as giving the book coherence; full set exemplified at 1 Kgs 22:41–43, 45, 50.
**Quote:** "With their general regularity of expression throughout Kings, the formulae contribute much to the book’s sense of coherence—to the sense that it “hangs together” as a single piece of work"
**Locus:** Intro Narrative; slice L237
**Targets:** [[1-2-kings]], [[kingship-in-israel]], [[iain-provan]]

### C-R0-12
**Claim:** Provan records ancient tradition ascribing Kings to a single author, the prophet Jeremiah (b. B. Bat. 15a).
**Quote:** "In fact, ancient tradition ascribed the book to a single author—to the prophet Jeremiah (cf. b. B. Bat. 15a)."
**Locus:** Intro Narrative; slice L237
**Targets:** [[1-2-kings]], [[iain-provan]]

### C-R0-13
**Claim:** Provan summarizes modern scholarly consensus: doubt of single authorship; greater/lesser incoherence (inconsistencies, repetitions, style/language variation) suggests the compiler was constrained by sources and/or that the original work was expanded by editor(s); result is a composite work over time with more or less conflicting voices.
**Quote:** "What we have in Kings, then, is a composite work, put together over a period of time by a number of authors or editors, its various parts speaking with more or less conflicting voices."
**Locus:** Intro Narrative; slice L239
**Targets:** [[1-2-kings]], [[deuteronomistic-history]], [[iain-provan]]

### C-R0-14
**Claim:** Provan criticizes modern academic practice: abundant source/redaction hypotheses and theology of putative editors, but scarce (until the last decade before his writing) reading of Kings in final form as narrative; commentaries often privilege pre-incorporation meanings, “original” vs late glosses, background, geography, flora/fauna over the complete story as it stands.
**Quote:** "Of the reading of the book as it stands as a complete story there has been, until recently, scarcely any."
**Locus:** Intro Narrative; slice L241
**Targets:** [[1-2-kings]], [[deuteronomistic-history]], [[iain-provan]], [[provan-1-2-kings-nibc]]

### C-R0-15
**Claim:** Provan challenges the fundamental assertion of incoherence: repetition can be literary artistry; style variation need not mean multiple authors; “inconsistent” often labels what might be theologically complex or ironic; OT scholars lacking literary competence may have found what presuppositions led them to expect.
**Quote:** "Repetition can, after all, be an aspect of literary artistry. Variation in style and language can have many explanations other than difference in authorship. “Inconsistent” is a word often used where terms such as “theologically complex” or “ironic” would do just as well."
**Locus:** Intro Narrative; slice L243
**Targets:** [[1-2-kings]], [[iain-provan]], [[deuteronomistic-history]]

### C-R0-16
**Claim:** Encouraged by recent Hebrew-narrative work that eschews speculation about growth history and reads texts “just as they are,” Provan sets out to read Kings as a unified whole—without thereby asserting single authorship at one frozen moment.
**Quote:** "Encouraged by recent work of this kind, and by my own reading of Hebrew texts, to believe that the trouble with Kings does indeed lie with the readers and not with the text, I have certainly set out in this commentary to read the book of Kings as a unified whole."
**Locus:** Intro Narrative; slice L247
**Targets:** [[1-2-kings]], [[iain-provan]], [[provan-1-2-kings-nibc]]

### C-R0-17
**Claim:** Provan’s compositional model: OT books generally grew gradually in dialogue with each other (high intertextuality—shared text blocks, quotation, evocative parallel storytelling); he prefers “authors” (plural) for human forces behind Kings, yet assumes they were not victims of sources or incompetence but ordered and crafted material as intended, for cumulative reading beginning to end.
**Quote:** "My working assumption, nevertheless, has been that these “authors” have not been the victims either of their sources or of their own incompetence. They have presented the material that they wanted to present, ordered and crafted in the way they wanted to do it"
**Locus:** Intro Narrative; slice L247–249
**Targets:** [[1-2-kings]], [[iain-provan]], [[deuteronomistic-history]]

### C-R0-18
**Claim:** Examples of intertextuality Provan cites for Kings: 2 Kgs 18:17–20:19 // Isa 36:1–38:8; 38:21–39:8; 2 Kgs 24:18–25:30 // Jer 52:1–34; 1 Kgs 22:28 and Mic 1:2; plus narrative evocation of other stories.
**Quote:** "the way in which individual books either share portions of text with other books (e.g., 2 Kgs. 18:17–20:19 and Isa. 36:1–38:8; 38:21–39:8; 2 Kgs. 24:18–25:30 and Jer. 52:1–34), or quote them (e.g., 1 Kgs. 22:28 and Mic. 1:2)"
**Locus:** Intro Narrative; slice L247
**Targets:** [[1-2-kings]], [[iain-provan]], [[hezekiah]]

### C-R0-19
**Claim:** Provan’s working assumption that problems in the text may be problems with the reader’s understanding yields, for him, Kings as carefully crafted and coherent—“The story ‘works.’ It does not need tinkering to make it do so.”
**Quote:** "When such an assumption is brought to the text, together with a commitment to consider it possible that “problems in the text” may actually be “problems with my understanding of the text,” I believe that the book of Kings can indeed be seen as a carefully crafted and coherent entity. The story “works.” It does not need tinkering to make it do so."
**Locus:** Intro Narrative; slice L249
**Targets:** [[1-2-kings]], [[iain-provan]], [[provan-1-2-kings-nibc]]

### C-R0-20
**Claim:** Provan links modern fragmentation of the Bible-story as Western culture’s defining narrative to loss of a sense of Scripture, including in the church’s treatment of the OT (plundered for NT illustrations; coherence supplied from outside rather than drawn from the story; interest in “behind” the text over “in” it)—even among conservatives who affirm inspiration.
**Quote:** "Even conservative commentaries on the OT narrative books tend to supply coherence to the story from elsewhere, rather than drawing it out of the story itself. They show little interest in reading the text as a text—even though they assert most firmly that it is a text inspired by God himself."
**Locus:** Intro Narrative; slice L251
**Targets:** [[iain-provan]], [[provan-1-2-kings-nibc]], [[1-2-kings]]

### C-R0-21
**Claim:** For those claiming orthodox Christian tradition, Provan says recovery of the OT as Scripture is of utmost importance; this commentary is “a small step” and is primarily a commentary on Kings as narrative literature.
**Quote:** "This commentary is intended as a small step in that direction. It is therefore a commentary primarily on the book of Kings as narrative literature."
**Locus:** Intro Narrative; slice L253
**Targets:** [[provan-1-2-kings-nibc]], [[iain-provan]], [[1-2-kings]]

### C-R0-22
**Claim:** Provan notes many literary readers who recover narrative power still resist treating history-like biblical narrative as about the real past, framing it as a self-referential “fictive world”; he explains this partly as desire to protect the text from historicist “Philistines” who treat it as a quarry for facts rather than a story.
**Quote:** "Yet they resist the idea that the narrative world thus portrayed has anything to do with the “real” world of the past. It is, rather, a “fictive world,” entire in itself and referring only to itself."
**Locus:** Intro “The Book of Kings as Historiographical Literature”; slice L257–259
**Targets:** [[1-2-kings]], [[iain-provan]]

### C-R0-23
**Claim:** Provan also critiques “newer historians” who sharply separate “biblical Israel” (literary, ideologically slanted construct, not starting point for serious history) from “historical Israel” (Palestinian highlands material culture, inscriptions, social theory)—aiming to replace “fiction” with “facts.”
**Quote:** "It has become fashionable to distinguish quite self-consciously between “biblical Israel” and “historical Israel.” … “Biblical Israel,” on the other hand—the Israel presented to us in the OT—is a literary construct. It has some points of contact with the past, but it is so ideologically slanted that it cannot serve as the starting point for serious historical enquiry."
**Locus:** Intro Historiographical; slice L261
**Targets:** [[1-2-kings]], [[iain-provan]]

### C-R0-24
**Claim:** Against text/history separation, Provan insists Kings has historiographical intent: it looks back to events and characters of the past and seeks to tell about the real world God has made and in which God acts—not only a fictive world—though literary conventions (e.g. names and numbers) must be considered when correlating text and history.
**Quote:** "First, it is clear that a book like Kings has historiographical intent. It looks, not only sideways at the other books of the OT but also back to the events and characters of the past. It seeks to tell us, not about a fictive world, but about the real world that God has made and in which God acts."
**Locus:** Intro Historiographical; slice L263
**Targets:** [[1-2-kings]], [[iain-provan]]

### C-R0-25
**Claim:** Provan argues all historiography (ancient or modern) is story-like and ideological (selection and persuasion) without thereby being incapable of speaking truly about the past; “newer historians” show selective skepticism—maximum suspicion of biblical witness, often uncritical faith in modern archaeological/sociological narratives—smuggling a non-religious confessionalism after expelling religious commitment.
**Quote:** "A selective skepticism is at work here. The biblical stories about Israel, on the one hand, are approached with the maximum degree of suspicion in regard to the extent to which they truly reflect what happened. There is, on the other hand, a touching degree of (sometimes quite uncritical) faith displayed when it comes to modern narratives about this same entity."
**Locus:** Intro Historiographical; slice L265
**Targets:** [[1-2-kings]], [[iain-provan]]

### C-R0-26
**Claim:** For Provan, Kings is a highly selective Iron Age portrait—long periods brief, short periods expansive—only one view among many possible, yet no less valuable as witness; authors neither tell nor claim to tell everything that happened.
**Quote:** "Kings is a highly selective account, in which fairly long periods can be passed over briefly and periods of a year or less can occupy quite a bit of space. It is a particular view of the past, with its own highlights and its own persuasive appeal—only one portrait of what happened, but no less valuable as a witness to the past for that."
**Locus:** Intro Historiographical; slice L267
**Targets:** [[1-2-kings]], [[iain-provan]]

### C-R0-27
**Claim:** From a Christian-Scripture stance, Provan holds Kings and Chronicles as the two “authorized portraits” of this period for church life and faith (citing 2 Tim 3:16); other reconstructions are “simply of academic interest”; the exegete’s task is not to re-paint Kings in modern colors that exclude divine action/miracle and privilege extra-biblical witnesses as “more historical.”
**Quote:** "This person will want to say that this portrait is one of two concerning this period of Israelite history that God has given the church for use in “teaching, rebuking, correcting and training in righteousness” (2 Tim. 3:16). It is one of the authorized portraits of Israel’s past (Chronicles is the other) so far as life and faith are concerned"
**Locus:** Intro Historiographical; slice L269
**Targets:** [[1-2-kings]], [[iain-provan]], [[provan-1-2-kings-nibc]]

### C-R0-28
**Claim:** Provan’s summary conviction on authority and history: the text (portrait), not the history behind the text (subject painted), is authoritative for the Church—yet historical referentiality cannot be dodged; Kings must be taken seriously as narrative about Israel’s past.
**Quote:** "In summary, my conviction is that, although it is the text that is authoritative for the Church and not the history behind the text—the portrait and not the subject painted—the question of historical referentiality cannot be dodged. Kings must be taken seriously as a narrative about Israel’s past."
**Locus:** Intro Historiographical; slice L273
**Targets:** [[1-2-kings]], [[iain-provan]], [[provan-1-2-kings-nibc]]

### C-R0-29
**Claim:** As didactic literature, Kings narrates Israel’s past so readers learn from it (Rom 15:4; 1 Cor 10:11), not for detached information alone.
**Quote:** "the book of Kings tells us about Israel’s past, not so that we should become better informed about it in some abstract, intellectually detached way, but so that we should learn from it (Rom. 15:4; 1 Cor. 10:11)."
**Locus:** Intro “The Book of Kings as Didactic Literature”; slice L277
**Targets:** [[1-2-kings]], [[iain-provan]]

### C-R0-30
**Claim:** Provan’s plot summary opens with succession struggle: Solomon over Adonijah; David’s instructions—keep the law of Moses so the LORD keeps the everlasting-dynasty promise, and act as a man of wisdom; the Solomon narrative (2:12–11:43) is constructed around wisdom and law.
**Quote:** "Solomon emerges victorious over Adonijah and is given instructions by David about how he should rule (1 Kgs. 1:1–2:11). He should keep the law of Moses, so that the LORD will keep his promise to David of an everlasting dynasty over Israel, and he should act as a man of wisdom. The succeeding narrative is constructed around these two ideas of wisdom and law (2:12–11:43)."
**Locus:** Intro Didactic story summary; slice L279
**Targets:** [[solomon]], [[david]], [[davidic-covenant]], [[succession-narrative]], [[1-2-kings]], [[iain-provan]]

### C-R0-31
**Claim:** In Provan’s reading of Solomon: wisdom often positive (prosperity, peace, temple) but also self-interested (eliminating threats, accumulating wealth); commitment to the LORD questioned from the start and ends in other gods; yet disobedience does not end the Davidic dynasty—punishment deferred to the son, who loses only part of the kingdom; northern alienation temporary.
**Quote:** "Surprisingly, however, his disobedience does not lead to the end of the Davidic dynasty. A prophet announces that punishment will be deferred until the days of his son, who is to lose only part of the kingdom, rather than all of it. This alienation of northern Israel from David will itself not last forever. It is only a temporary phenomenon."
**Locus:** Intro Didactic story summary; slice L279
**Targets:** [[solomon]], [[davidic-covenant]], [[1-2-kings]], [[iain-provan]]

### C-R0-32
**Claim:** Provan summarizes the northern story as “exodus into slavery”: Jeroboam’s independence becomes captivity to other gods (Jeroboam’s gods and foreign imports); prophets oppose apostate kings; Elijah and Elisha dominate 1 Kgs 17–2 Kgs 13, mitigating wrath and offering salvation in judgment; final northern exile to Assyria (2 Kgs 17) delayed by God’s promises and compassion (2 Kgs 10:30; 13:23).
**Quote:** "The most notable of these prophets are Elijah and Elisha, whose activities take up a substantial part of the narrative throughout 1 Kings 17–2 Kings 13. They themselves in some respects mitigate the full force of God’s wrath upon Israel, offering salvation in the midst of judgment."
**Locus:** Intro Didactic story summary; slice L281
**Targets:** [[elijah]], [[elisha]], [[1-2-kings]], [[iain-provan]]

### C-R0-33
**Claim:** Provan’s Judah summary: not continuous apostasy after a bad start; relatively good kings and two of the “very best” reformers/trusters (2 Kgs 18:1ff.; 22:1ff.—Hezekiah and Josiah in the book’s frame); commitment to David delays but does not avert judgment; Manasseh’s sins tip the scale (2 Kgs 21); Babylonian exile; Davidic future hangs by Jehoiachin at the Babylonian king’s table (25:27–30).
**Quote:** "The future of the Davidic line apparently hangs by the slender thread of a displaced ruler sitting at the table of the king of Babylon (25:27–30)."
**Locus:** Intro Didactic story summary; slice L283
**Targets:** [[hezekiah]], [[davidic-covenant]], [[1-2-kings]], [[david]], [[iain-provan]]

### C-R0-34
**Claim:** Theme 1 in Provan’s theology of Kings: the LORD alone is God—not human-created gods; incomparable Creator, distinct from creation yet active in it; controls nature and history; prophets announce the future God brings about; prophetic word not hinderable, though God in freedom can override fulfilment for divine purposes.
**Quote:** "It is God, and neither god, nor king, nor prophet, who controls history … Nothing can hinder the fulfilment of this prophetic word—although God in divine freedom can override its fulfilment for divine purposes (1 Kgs. 21:17–29; 2 Kgs. 3:15–27)."
**Locus:** Intro Didactic themes; slice L285
**Targets:** [[1-2-kings]], [[iain-provan]]

### C-R0-35
**Claim:** Theme 2: exclusive worship demanded of Israelite and foreigner; main concern is content (no idols/images; not fertility/“nations” cults); subsidiary concern is place (ideally Jerusalem temple, not high places); false worship entails moral wrong; true worship bound to law; true wisdom defined by true worship and obedience (1 Kgs 1–11)—worship and ethics as two sides of one coin.
**Quote:** "Worship and ethics are two sides of the same coin, in Kings as elsewhere in the OT."
**Locus:** Intro Didactic themes; slice L287
**Targets:** [[1-2-kings]], [[kingship-in-israel]], [[iain-provan]]

### C-R0-36
**Claim:** Theme 3: God judges wrongdoers (kings, prophets, ordinary Israelites), but Kings is “not a vending-machine world” of neat sin–retribution correlation; the compassionate Judge delays/mitigates; grace confounds expectations formed on the basis of law; yet sin can accumulate so judgment sweeps cultures, relatively innocent with guilty.
**Quote:** "It is not a vending-machine world, however, in which every coin of sin that is inserted results in individually packaged retribution. There is no neat correlation between sin and judgment in Kings"
**Locus:** Intro Didactic themes; slice L289
**Targets:** [[1-2-kings]], [[iain-provan]]

### C-R0-37
**Claim:** Theme 4—promise—at the heart of the LORD’s gracious behavior; most prominent is the eternal-dynasty promise to David, in paradoxical form: often unconditional explanation of Davidic survival despite disobedience (1 Kgs 11:36; 15:4; 2 Kgs 8:19), at other times conditioned on successors’ obedience (1 Kgs 2:4; 8:25; 9:4–5).
**Quote:** "The most prominent of the promises in Kings is God’s promise to David of an eternal dynasty. It appears in a curiously paradoxical form."
**Locus:** Intro Didactic themes; slice L291
**Targets:** [[davidic-covenant]], [[david]], [[1-2-kings]], [[iain-provan]]

### C-R0-38
**Claim:** Provan’s narrative of the Davidic promise under stress: conditional aspect seemingly prevails as sin accumulates and Judah is judged like Israel—yet Jehoiachin lives (2 Kgs 25:27–30), like Joash before him (2 Kgs 11), holding out recovery of the Davidic line and the possibility that the promise transcends sin after all (cf. 1 Kgs 11:39); grace may triumph over law.
**Quote:** "And yet, Jehoiachin lives (2 Kgs. 25:27–30). His survival in the midst of near total disaster, like that of Joash before him (2 Kgs. 11), holds out the possibility of recovery for the Davidic line—the possibility that the promise transcends sin after all and that David will indeed rule again over all Israel, as 1 Kings 11:39 implies."
**Locus:** Intro Didactic themes; slice L291
**Targets:** [[davidic-covenant]], [[david]], [[1-2-kings]], [[iain-provan]]

### C-R0-39
**Claim:** Provan pairs the Davidic promise with the promise to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob (descendants; everlasting land possession) as also shaping God’s treatment of the people (2 Kgs 13:23; implicitly 1 Kgs 4:20–21, 24; 18:36) and standing behind Solomon’s prayer for post-judgment forgiveness (1 Kgs 8:22–53); grace may not be presumed upon but hoped for from God’s character and promises.

### C-R0-40
**Claim:** Provan insists Christian readers must read Kings within Genesis–Revelation and especially in light of Jesus Christ as the story’s center, without emptying the OT of its own theological significance or reducing it to a NT-bestowed meaning only; OT provides theological (not merely historical) context for the NT as well as being read in its light.
**Quote:** "This does not mean (as it has sometimes been taken to mean in the past) that Kings has no theological significance of its own and that its meaning is entirely bestowed upon it by the NT. That is not to take the OT seriously as Scripture."

### C-R0-41
**Claim:** Provan’s typology: biblical story is patterned so later events/characters recall earlier ones; within Kings (Judah’s kings vs David; Jeroboam as Moses then Aaron; Manasseh and Josiah both recalling Ahab); NT tells Jesus’ story in ways that recall Kings thematically and in character/event; Kings functions typologically toward the NT story and toward NT-addressed readers who attach their lives to its narrative.
**Quote:** "The story of Kings, in other words, functions typologically in respect of the later NT story, preparing its way and gaining full significance only when read with it in mind. It also functions typologically in respect of the persons addressed by the NT (i.e., us, the readers)."
**Locus:** Intro Didactic / typology; slice L295
**Targets:** [[1-2-kings]], [[david]], [[kingship-in-israel]], [[iain-provan]]

### C-R0-42
**Claim:** Commentary practice for typology: NT cross-references where reflection is especially significant; four excursuses on major characters in canonical context (§§18, 34, 46, 57); scripture index aids preaching/teaching; the commentary (like Kings) is designed to be read through, not raided—“It exists not to be raided but to be read!”
**Quote:** "The commentary is designed, however—like the book upon which it comments—to be read all the way through, rather than simply dipped into here and there, and it is only engagement with the whole book of Kings that will truly communicate its distinctive message. **Locus:** Intro closing; slice L297

- **Deuteronomistic History (DH):** The Introduction critiques multi-author/editor, source-constrained, conflicting-voices models of Kings and the academic preference for redaction/source over final-form narrative. Provan does **not** use the phrase “Deuteronomistic History” or name Noth/Dtr in this slice.
